nodes.title: Smooth approximation within the simplex
nodes.statement: For F∈𝒮_k and δ>0 there is a smooth F₁∈𝒮_k, supported on ℛ_k, with I_k(F₁) > 0 and ratio(F₁) > ratio(F) − δ. In particular M_k is also the supremum over smooth functions supported on ℛ_k.
hypotheses: 𝒮_k is the L² class of SV.4/maynard-functionals.
proofSteps: Shrink: F_η(t) = F((t − η𝟙)/(1 − (k+1)η)) vanishes unless tᵢ ≥ η and Σtᵢ ≤ 1 − η. I scales by (1 − (k+1)η)^k and each J^{(m)} by (1 − (k+1)η)^{k+1}, so the ratio is multiplied by 1 − (k+1)η.
Mollify: convolve F_η with a smooth bump (Mathlib ContDiffBump) of radius below η/√k. The result is smooth, supported in ℛ_k, and converges to F_η in L²(cube) as the radius tends to 0.

Continuity: F ↦ ∫_0^1 F dt_m is 1-Lipschitz from L²(cube) to L²(cube) by Cauchy–Schwarz, so I and each J^{(m)} are continuous. For η and the radius small enough, the ratio moves by less than δ and I and the J^{(m)} stay nonzero.
acceptance: Maynard's proof of Proposition 4.2 uses this step without proof; it is supplied here.

sources.match: The approximation step. The proof is worker-derived.

nodes.title: The GPY positivity criterion
nodes.statement: Let H be finite, N∈ℕ, w_n ≥ 0 and ρ∈ℝ. If Σ_{N≤n<2N} (#{h∈H : n+h prime} − ρ)w_n > 0, then some n∈[N,2N) has more than ρ, hence at least ⌊ρ+1⌋, of the n+h prime.
hypotheses: No arithmetic input. The weights need only be nonnegative.
proofSteps: If every n had at most ρ of the n+h prime, each summand (#{…} − ρ)w_n would be ≤ 0, because w_n ≥ 0, and so would the sum.
An integer c > ρ satisfies c ≥ ⌊ρ⌋ + 1 = ⌊ρ + 1⌋.
acceptance: With ρ = θM_k/2 − ε this is the positivity step of Proposition 4.2. For small ε>0, ⌊ρ+1⌋ = ⌈θM_k/2⌉.

sources.match: The criterion.

nodes.title: Size of λ in terms of y (Maynard (5.9))
nodes.statement: If y vanishes off the support (∏rᵢ squarefree, coprime to W, less than R) and |y_r| ≤ y_max, then |λ_d| ≤ y_max Σ_{u<R} μ²(u)τ_k(u)/φ(u) for every d. The right-hand side is O_k(y_max (log R)^k).
hypotheses: τ_k(u) is the number of ordered factorizations u = c₁⋯c_k.
proofSteps: Insert |y_r| ≤ y_max into (5.8) and write rᵢ = dᵢr′ᵢ. Since ∏rᵢ is squarefree, the r′ᵢ are coprime to ∏dᵢ.
Use d/φ(d) = Σ_{e|d} 1/φ(e) for squarefree d and the multiplicativity of φ to combine everything into Σ_{u<R} μ²(u)τ_k(u)/φ(u), with u = dr′ and τ_k(dr′) ≥ τ_k(r′) (5.9).

Σ_{u<R} μ²(u)τ_k(u)/φ(u) ≤ ∏_{p<R}(1 + k/(p−1)) ≤ exp(k Σ_{p<R} 1/(p−1)) = O_k((log R)^k). This uses Σ_{p<R} 1/p = log log R + O(1), which follows from Mertens' first theorem (requested from AN.2) by partial summation.
acceptance: The O_k((log R)^k) bound is what turns the error O(λ_max²R²(log R)^{2k}) of (5.3) into O(y_max²R²(log R)^{4k}).

sources.match: The bound. The final Mertens estimate is made explicit here.

nodes.title: Diagonal form of S₁ (Maynard Lemma 5.1)
nodes.statement: Let y vanish off the support, with |y_r| ≤ y_max, and λ = λ(y). Then S₁ = (N/W) Σ_r y_r²/∏φ(rᵢ) + O(y_max² φ(W)^k N(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
proofSteps: Expand the square and swap the sums (5.1). By the Chinese remainder theorem, the count of N≤n<2N with n≡v₀ (W) and [dᵢ,eᵢ] | n+hᵢ is N/q + O(1), q = W∏[dᵢ,eᵢ], when W, [d₁,e₁], …, [d_k,e_k] are pairwise coprime. Otherwise it is 0: a prime dividing [dᵢ,eᵢ] and [dⱼ,eⱼ] divides hᵢ − hⱼ and exceeds D₀ > max|hᵢ − hⱼ| (5.2).
The O(1) terms: λ is supported on ∏dᵢ < R, so they total ≪ λ_max²(Σ_{d<R} τ_k(d))² ≪ λ_max²R²(log R)^{2k} (5.3), with λ_max ≪ y_max(log R)^k (SV.4/lambda-max-bound).
Main term: 1/[dᵢ,eᵢ] = (dᵢeᵢ)^{−1} Σ_{uᵢ|dᵢ,eᵢ} φ(uᵢ) (5.4). Remove the remaining conditions (dᵢ,eⱼ) = 1 (i≠j) with Möbius sums over s_{i,j}, restricted as in the source (5.5)–(5.6).

Substitute the change of variables (5.7)–(5.8) to get (5.11). Every s_{i,j} ≠ 1 is coprime to W, hence exceeds D₀; these terms contribute O(y_max²φ(W)^kN(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)) (5.12), using Σ_{u<R,(u,W)=1} μ²(u)/φ(u) ≪ (φ(W)/W) log R (SV.1/selberg-diagonal-sum-dimension-one).
R² ≤ N^{1−2δ} and W ≪ N^δ, so the O(y_max²R²(log R)^{4k}) error is smaller than the first (5.13).
acceptance: The main term is diagonal in y: the change of variables diagonalizes the quadratic form S₁, as in the main term of Selberg's one-dimensional sieve (compare Mathlib's lambdaSquared).

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Diagonal form of S₂^{(m)} (Maynard Lemma 5.2)
nodes.statement: Assume in addition that the primes have level of distribution θ, that k ≥ 2, and fix A>0. Then S₂^{(m)} = N/(φ(W) log N) Σ_r (y^{(m)}_r)²/∏g(rᵢ) + O((y^{(m)}_max)² φ(W)^{k−2}N(log N)^{k−2}/(W^{k−1}D₀)) + O(y_max² N/(log N)^A).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
y^{(m)}_max bounds |y^{(m)}_r| for every r.
proofSteps: Expand as for S₁ (5.15). The inner sum runs over one class mod q = W∏[dᵢ,eᵢ] and is coprime to q exactly when d_m = e_m = 1. It equals X_N/φ(q) + O(E(N,q)), where X_N = #{N≤n<2N : n prime} and E is windowError (5.16)–(5.18).

Error: q is squarefree and less than R²W, and each q arises from at most τ_{3k}(q) tuples. With λ_max ≪ y_max(log R)^k the error is ≪ y_max²(log R)^{2k} Σ_{q<R²W} μ²(q)τ_{3k}(q)E(N,q). Cauchy–Schwarz with E(N,q) ≪ N/φ(q) and PrimesHaveLevel.sum_windowError (R²W < N^{θ−δ} for large N) give ≪ y_max²N/(log N)^A (5.19)–(5.20).

Main term: write 1/φ([dᵢ,eᵢ]) = (φ(dᵢ)φ(eᵢ))^{−1} Σ_{uᵢ|dᵢ,eᵢ} g(uᵢ) (5.21), remove the cross coprimality with Möbius sums, and substitute y^{(m)} (5.23) to get (5.24). Terms with s_{i,j} ≠ 1 contribute the D₀ error (5.25).
Replace X_N by N/log N + O(N/(log N)²), by the prime number theorem (requested from AN.2); the error is absorbed (5.26)–(5.27).
acceptance: This is the only use of the arithmetic hypothesis. Unconditional results come from SV.3/bombieri-vinogradov-level.
The implied constants are ineffective through Bombieri–Vinogradov (remark after Lemma 5.2).

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: y^{(m)} in terms of y (Maynard Lemma 5.3)
nodes.statement: If r_m = 1, then y^{(m)}_r = Σ_{a_m} y_{r₁,…,r_{m−1},a_m,r_{m+1},…,r_k}/φ(a_m) + O(y_max φ(W) log R/(W D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
proofSteps: Substitute (5.8) into (5.23) (5.28), then swap the d and a sums (5.29).
Evaluate Σ_{rᵢ|dᵢ|aᵢ} μ(dᵢ)dᵢ/φ(dᵢ) = μ(aᵢ)rᵢ/φ(aᵢ) for squarefree aᵢ (5.30).
Since (aⱼ,W) = 1, either aⱼ = rⱼ or aⱼ > D₀rⱼ. The terms with aⱼ > D₀rⱼ contribute O(y_max φ(W) log R/(WD₀)), using Σ_{a_m<R,(a_m,W)=1} μ²(a_m)/φ(a_m) ≪ (φ(W)/W) log R (5.31).
When aⱼ = rⱼ for every j≠m, the factor ∏g(rᵢ)rᵢ/φ(rᵢ)² is 1 + O(1/D₀), because g(p)p/φ(p)² = 1 − 1/(p−1)² and every prime factor exceeds D₀ (5.32).
acceptance: y^{(m)} vanishes unless r_m = 1; the lemma is the only link between y^{(m)} and y.

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Asymptotic for S₁ (Maynard Lemma 6.2)
nodes.statement: S₁ = φ(W)^k N(log R)^k I_k(F)/W^{k+1} + O(F_max² φ(W)^k N(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
F is of class C¹ and supported on ℛ_k, and F_max = sup_{[0,1]^k} (|F| + Σᵢ|∂F/∂tᵢ|); y = y(F) is given by (6.3).
proofSteps: Insert (6.3) into Lemma 5.1 (6.4); y_max ≤ F_max.
Drop the pairwise coprimality of the uᵢ: two integers coprime to W with a common factor share a prime greater than D₀. This costs O(F_max²φ(W)^kN(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)) (6.5).
Apply SV.1/selberg-smooth-diagonal-sum k times, once in each variable, with γ(p) = 1 for p∤W and γ(p) = 0 for p|W. Then c_γ = φ(W)/W and L ≪ 1 + Σ_{p|W} log p/p ≪ log D₀ by Mertens (6.7)–(6.9).
Combine: the error O(log D₀ (log R)^{k−1}) is smaller than (log R)^k/D₀.
acceptance: The main term is positive whenever I_k(F) ≠ 0.

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Asymptotic for S₂^{(m)} (Maynard Lemma 6.3)
nodes.statement: If the primes have level of distribution θ, then S₂^{(m)} = φ(W)^k N(log R)^{k+1} J_k^{(m)}(F)/(W^{k+1} log N) + O(F_max² φ(W)^k N(log R)^k/(W^{k+1}D₀)).
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
F is of class C¹ and supported on ℛ_k, and F_max = sup_{[0,1]^k} (|F| + Σᵢ|∂F/∂tᵢ|); y = y(F) is given by (6.3).
proofSteps: By Lemma 5.3 and (6.3): if r_m = 1 and ∏rᵢ is squarefree and coprime to W, then y^{(m)}_r = Σ_{(u,W∏rᵢ)=1} μ²(u)/φ(u)·F(…, log u/log R, …) + O(F_max φ(W) log R/(WD₀)) (6.10). In particular y^{(m)}_max ≪ φ(W)F_max log R/W.

Apply SV.1/selberg-smooth-diagonal-sum in u with γ(p) = 1 for p∤W∏rᵢ, where L ≪ log log N (6.11)–(6.12). This gives y^{(m)}_r = (log R)(φ(W)/W)∏(φ(rᵢ)/rᵢ)·F^{(m)}_r + O(…), where F^{(m)}_r = ∫_0^1 F(…, t_m, …) dt_m (6.13)–(6.14).
Substitute into Lemma 5.2 (6.15)–(6.16) and drop the coprimality of the rᵢ at the cost (6.17).
Apply SV.1/selberg-smooth-diagonal-sum to each rᵢ (i≠m) with γ(p) = 1 − (p²−3p+1)/(p³−p²−2p+1) for p∤W, for which γ(p)/(p−γ(p)) = φ(p)²/(g(p)p²) (6.19). The result is J_k^{(m)} (6.21)–(6.22).
acceptance: Check of (6.19): p(p−1)²/(p³−p²−2p+1) = 1 − (p²−3p+1)/(p³−p²−2p+1). arXiv v2 printed a different γ; v3 and the published text agree on this one.

sources.match: The lemma and the steps of its proof.

nodes.title: Maynard's asymptotics for S₁ and S₂ (Proposition 4.1)
nodes.statement: Let the primes have level of distribution θ∈(0,1], let R = N^{θ/2−δ} with δ>0 fixed, and let F be smooth and supported on ℛ_k with I_k(F) ≠ 0 and J_k^{(m)}(F) ≠ 0 for every m. With λ built from F: S₁ = (1+o(1)) φ(W)^k N(log R)^k I_k(F)/W^{k+1}, and for every m, S₂^{(m)} = (1+o(1)) φ(W)^k N(log R)^{k+1} J_k^{(m)}(F)/(W^{k+1} log N); hence S₂ = Σ_m S₂^{(m)} has the stated asymptotic.
hypotheses: N is large, D₀ = log log log N, W = ∏_{p≤D₀}p, v₀ is the W-trick residue of the admissible H = {h₁,…,h_k} (distinct), R = N^{θ/2−δ} with 0<θ≤1 and δ>0 fixed. The implied constants depend on k, H, θ and δ, and not on N, y or F.
Maynard states Proposition 4.1 with 'exponent of distribution θ'; it is the level of distribution of (1.3).
proofSteps: Apply Lemmas 6.2 and 6.3 with F fixed: F_max is a constant and D₀ → ∞, so each error term is o(main term), because I_k(F) and J_k^{(m)}(F) are nonzero.
The λ of Proposition 4.1 is the construction from (6.3), by the inversion (5.8).
acceptance: The S₂ asymptotic, summed over m, is Proposition 4.1's display with Σ_m J_k^{(m)}(F).

sources.match: The proposition. Its proof is §§5–6, decomposed in the lemmas above.

nodes.title: Primes in admissible tuples (Maynard Proposition 4.2)
nodes.statement: Let the primes have level of distribution θ∈(0,1] and let H = {h₁,…,h_k} be admissible. With r_k = ⌈θM_k/2⌉, there are infinitely many n such that at least r_k of n+h₁, …, n+h_k are prime. In particular liminf_n (p_{n+r_k−1} − p_n) ≤ max_{i,j}(hᵢ − hⱼ).
hypotheses: The hᵢ are distinct. M_k is the quantity of SV.4/maynard-functionals.
proofSteps: Choose F₀∈𝒮_k with ratio > M_k − δ, and then a smooth F₁ with ratio > M_k − 2δ (SV.4/ratio-smooth-approximation).

Proposition 4.1 for F₁ gives S = S₂ − ρS₁ = (φ(W)^kN(log R)^k I_k(F₁)/W^{k+1})·((log R/log N) Σ_m J^{(m)}(F₁) − ρI(F₁) + o(1)) ≥ (…)·((θ/2 − δ)(M_k − 2δ) − ρ + o(1)). This is (4.4), whose printed sum index j should be m (E27).

Take ρ = θM_k/2 − ε, with δ small in terms of ε. Then S > 0 for all large N. The weights are nonnegative, so the positivity criterion gives, for each large N, some n∈[N,2N) with at least ⌊ρ+1⌋ = ⌈θM_k/2⌉ of the n+hᵢ prime (ε small).
Since this holds for every large N, there are infinitely many such n. The gap statement is SV.4/clustered-primes-to-gaps.
acceptance: k = 105 and θ = 1/2 − ε give r₁₀₅ ≥ 2 (Theorem 1.3). k = 5 and θ = 1 − ε give r₅ ≥ 2 under Elliott–Halberstam (Theorem 1.4).

sources.match: The proposition and its proof.

planet.name: Maynard's refinement of the GPY sieve

nodes.title: From prime clusters to prime gaps
nodes.statement: Let H be finite and nonempty and r ≥ 1. If infinitely many n have at least r of the n+h (h∈H) prime, then p_{j+r−1} − p_j ≤ max H − min H for infinitely many j, i.e. liminf_j (p_{j+r−1} − p_j) ≤ max H − min H. Here p_j is the j-th prime, counted from 0.
hypotheses: Maynard's p_n is 1-indexed. Differences p_{n+m} − p_n are unaffected by the shift.
proofSteps: For such an n, let q₁ < … < q_r be r of the primes among the n+h, and let j be the index of q₁. The r primes lie in [q₁, q_r], so p_{j+r−1} ≤ q_r and p_{j+r−1} − p_j ≤ q_r − q₁ ≤ max H − min H.
Distinct large n give arbitrarily large q₁, hence infinitely many j.
acceptance: With r = 2 and H of diameter 600 this is the step from Proposition 4.2 to liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600.

sources.match: The deduction, which the source leaves implicit.

nodes.title: Lower bound for M_k when k is large (Maynard Proposition 4.3(3))
nodes.statement: For all sufficiently large k, M_k > log k − 2 log log k − 2.
hypotheses: The implied constants in §7 are independent of k.
proofSteps: Take F(t) = ∏g(ktᵢ) on ℛ_k (7.3), with g supported on [0,T], γ = ∫g², and μ = ∫ug²/γ < 1 − T/k (7.8). Then I_k ≤ k^{−k}γ^k (7.4), and J_k ≥ J′_k − E_k with J′_k = k^{−k−1}γ^{k−1}(∫g)² (7.5)–(7.7).

Bound E_k by a second moment. With η = (k−T)/(k−1) − μ > 0, 1 ≤ η^{−2}(Σ_{i≥2}uᵢ/(k−1) − μ)² on the error region (7.9). Drop the constraint Σ_{i=2}^k uᵢ > k−T (printed with i=1, E30) and expand the square: E_k ≤ η^{−2}μTk^{−k−1}γ^{k−1}(∫g)²/(k−1) (7.10)–(7.13).
Hence kJ_k/I_k ≥ ((∫g)²/∫g²)·(1 − T/(k(1 − T/k − μ)²)) (7.14). This uses (k−1)η² ≥ k(1 − T/k − μ)², which holds because η = x + (k−T)/(k(k−1)) with x = 1 − T/k − μ and 2(k−T)/k ≥ x.
Choose g(t) = 1/(1+At) on [0,T] with 1 + AT = e^A (7.16)–(7.18), and A = log k − 2 log log k (7.20)–(7.21).
acceptance: Only the leading term log k matters for Theorem 1.1. The −2 absorbs the loss log k/((log k)² + O(1)) in (7.21).

sources.match: The construction and estimates.

nodes.title: Moments on the simplex (Maynard Lemma 8.1, corrected)
nodes.statement: For integers k ≥ 1 and a, b, j ≥ 0: ∫_{ℛ_k} (1 − P₁)^a P_j^b dt = (a! b!/(k+a+jb)!) Σ_{b₁+…+b_k=b} ∏ᵢ (jbᵢ)!/bᵢ! = (a!/(k+jb+a)!)·G_{b,j}(k). Here P_j = Σtᵢ^j and G_{b,j}(x) = b! Σ_{r=0}^{b} C(x,r) Σ_{b₁,…,b_r≥1, Σbᵢ=b} ∏(jbᵢ)!/bᵢ!. The term r = 0, which makes G_{0,j} = 1, is needed; the printed formula starts at r = 1 (E31).
hypotheses: The multinomial form, summed over all (b₁,…,b_k) including zero entries, needs no convention at b = 0.
proofSteps: Dirichlet integral (8.2): ∫_{ℛ_k}(1−Σtᵢ)^a ∏tᵢ^{aᵢ} = a!∏aᵢ!/(k + a + Σaᵢ)!. Prove it by induction on k: integrate t₁ over [0, 1 − Σ_{i≥2}tᵢ] with v = t₁/(1 − Σ_{i≥2}tᵢ) and use the Beta integral ∫_0^1 t^a(1−t)^b dt = a!b!/(a+b+1)! (from Mathlib's Γ–Beta identity) (8.3).
Expand P_j^b by the multinomial theorem (8.4) and apply (8.2); this gives (8.5).
Group the tuples by the number r of nonzero bᵢ (8.6). For b = 0 the only tuple is zero, which is the r = 0 term.
acceptance: k = 5, a = 2, b = 0: the integral is 2!/7! = 1/2520, while the printed formula gives 0.

sources.match: The lemma, corrected at b = 0.

nodes.title: I_k and J_k as quadratic forms (Maynard Lemma 8.2)
nodes.statement: For P = Σ_{i=1}^d aᵢ(1 − P₁)^{bᵢ}P₂^{cᵢ} and F = P on ℛ_k (0 elsewhere), with k ≥ 2: I_k(F) = Σ_{i,j} aᵢaⱼ(bᵢ+bⱼ)! G_{cᵢ+cⱼ,2}(k)/(k+bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ)!, and J_k^{(m)}(F) = Σ_{i,j} aᵢaⱼ Σ_{c′₁≤cᵢ, c′₂≤cⱼ} C(cᵢ,c′₁)C(cⱼ,c′₂)·γ·G_{c′₁+c′₂,2}(k−1)/(k+bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ+1)!. Here γ = bᵢ!bⱼ!(2cᵢ−2c′₁)!(2cⱼ−2c′₂)!(bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ−2c′₁−2c′₂+2)!/((bᵢ+2cᵢ−2c′₁+1)!(bⱼ+2cⱼ−2c′₂+1)!), and G includes the r = 0 term (E31). So I_k and Σ_m J_k^{(m)} are quadratic forms aᵀA₁a and aᵀA₂a with rational A₁, A₂.
hypotheses: F is symmetric, so J_k^{(m)} does not depend on m and Σ_m J_k^{(m)} = kJ_k^{(1)}.
proofSteps: I_k: expand P² and apply the corrected Lemma 8.1 with j = 2 (8.7).
J: expand P₂^c = Σ C(c,c′)(P′₂)^{c′} t₁^{2c−2c′} and integrate in t₁ with the Beta integral (8.8); then square (8.9).

Apply Lemma 8.1 on ℛ_{k−1}: ∫_{ℛ_{k−1}}(1−P′₁)^B(P′₂)^{c′} = B! G_{c′,2}(k−1)/(k−1+B+2c′)!. The printed (8.10) has (k+b+c−1)! and G_{c,2} (E32). With B = bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ−2c′₁−2c′₂+2 the denominator is (k+bᵢ+bⱼ+2cᵢ+2cⱼ+1)!, as in the lemma.
acceptance: k = 5 with (8.16): exact rational arithmetic with these formulas gives I₅ = 29509/1222452000 and ratio 1417255/708216, which agrees with direct integration. The printed G (r ≥ 1) gives I₅ = 17753/977961600 and ratio 26784/17753 ≈ 1.509.
By Lemma 8.3 the best ratio in the span is the largest eigenvalue of A₁^{−1}A₂. A lower bound for M_k needs only one explicit coefficient vector.

sources.match: The lemma. The printed statement is right once G is corrected; (8.10) is corrected.

nodes.title: M₅ > 2 (Maynard Proposition 4.3(1))
proofSteps: F is bounded and supported on ℛ₅, with I ≠ 0 and every J^{(m)} ≠ 0, so it is admissible.
Lemma 8.2 with these four monomials gives I₅(F) = 29509/1222452000, Σ_m J₅^{(m)}(F) = 5J₅^{(1)}(F), and the ratio exactly 1417255/708216 (8.17).
maynardRatio_le_maynardM.
acceptance: 1417255/708216 ≈ 2.00115. The exact value was recomputed here, both by direct Dirichlet-integral expansion and by the corrected Lemma 8.2.
θM₅/2 > 1 needs θ > 2·708216/1417255 ≈ 0.99942, which is why Theorem 1.4 needs Elliott–Halberstam.

sources.match: The polynomial and the exact ratio.

nodes.title: M₁₀₅ > 4 (Maynard Proposition 4.3(2))
nodes.statement: M₁₀₅ > 4.
hypotheses: P is a linear combination of the 42 monomials (1−P₁)^bP₂^c with b + 2c ≤ 11, and k = 105.
proofSteps: Form the 42×42 rational matrices A₁, A₂ of Lemma 8.2 at k = 105.

The largest eigenvalue of A₁^{−1}A₂ is ≈ 4.0020697 (8.15). Instead of bounding an eigenvalue, take a rational approximation a of the eigenvector and check aᵀA₂a > 4aᵀA₁a in exact arithmetic, as the source suggests.
maynardRatio_le_maynardM.
acceptance: Recomputed here: the largest eigenvalue is 4.00206976…, and a rational coefficient vector (denominators 10^60) gives an exact ratio 4.0020697619… > 4.
(1/2 − ε)M₁₀₅/2 > 1 for small ε: this is the input of Theorem 1.3.

sources.match: The computation and its exact-arithmetic verification.

nodes.title: Engelsma's admissible 105-tuple of diameter 600
nodes.statement: The 105-element set H₁₀₅ = {0, 10, 12, 24, 28, …, 594, 598, 600} of Maynard's footnote 2 is admissible, contains 0 and 600, and lies in [0,600].
hypotheses: The set is copied in full into the suggested Lean file.
proofSteps: By isAdmissible_iff_card_image_lt, only the 27 primes p ≤ 103 need checking. For each, exhibit a missed residue: for example 1 mod 2, 2 mod 3, 1 mod 5, 4 mod 7, 7 mod 11 and 6 mod 13.
This is a finite, decidable computation.
acceptance: Recomputed here: the 105 elements are distinct and sorted, the set is admissible, and its diameter is 600. The list in the published text agrees with arXiv v3.

sources.match: The set; Maynard attributes it to Engelsma's computations.

nodes.title: The first k primes above k are admissible
nodes.statement: For every k, the first k primes greater than k form an admissible set. Its diameter p_{π(k)+k} − p_{π(k)+1} is O(k log k).
hypotheses: In 0-indexed form the set is {nth prime (π(k) + i) : i < k}.
proofSteps: Every element is a prime greater than k, so none is divisible by a prime p ≤ k = #H; apply isAdmissible_of_forall_not_dvd. The published argument says 'less than k', and so omits p = k when k is prime (E29).
Diameter: π(k) + k ≤ 2k, and Chebyshev's lower bound π(x) ≥ c·x/log x (Mathlib pi_ge') gives p_n ≪ n log n.
acceptance: k = 5: {7, 11, 13, 17, 19}. It misses 0 mod 5 because no element is divisible by 5; this is the case p = k.

sources.match: The set and its diameter. The admissibility argument is corrected at p = k.

nodes.title: Bounded gaps between primes (Maynard Theorem 1.3)
nodes.statement: liminf_n (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600.
hypotheses: Unconditional. It uses Bombieri–Vinogradov and none of Zhang's technology.
proofSteps: Bombieri–Vinogradov gives level θ = 1/2 − ε. Since M₁₀₅ > 4, θM₁₀₅/2 > 1 for small ε, so r₁₀₅ = ⌈θM₁₀₅/2⌉ ≥ 2.
Proposition 4.2 with Engelsma's admissible H₁₀₅ (diameter 600): infinitely many n have two primes among the n + H₁₀₅. Hence liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 600.
acceptance: This is not the twin prime conjecture, and 600 is not optimal (Maynard, p. 385).

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: Gaps under Elliott–Halberstam (Maynard Theorem 1.4)
nodes.statement: If the primes have level of distribution θ for every θ < 1 (the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture), then liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 12 and liminf(p_{n+2} − p_n) ≤ 600.
hypotheses: Conditional on the named hypothesis ElliottHalberstam of SV.3/level-of-distribution.
proofSteps: k = 105 and θ = 1 − ε: θM₁₀₅/2 > 2, so three primes occur among n + H₁₀₅ infinitely often, and liminf(p_{n+2} − p_n) ≤ 600.
k = 5, H = {0,2,6,8,12} (admissible, diameter 12) and θ = 1 − ε: θM₅/2 > 1, so liminf(p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 12.
acceptance: 12 appears to be optimal for the method in its current form (Maynard, p. 385).

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: m + 1 primes in bounded intervals (Maynard Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant C such that liminf_n (p_{n+m} − p_n) ≤ C m³ e^{4m} for every m ≥ 1.
hypotheses: Unconditional.
proofSteps: Take θ = 1/2 − 1/k (Bombieri–Vinogradov). By Proposition 4.3(3), θM_k/2 ≥ (1/4 − 1/(2k))(log k − 2 log log k − 2) (4.5), which exceeds m once k ≥ C₀m²e^{4m} for an absolute C₀.
Take k = ⌈C₀m²e^{4m}⌉ and H the first k primes above k, which is admissible with diameter ≪ k log k.
Proposition 4.2 gives m + 1 primes among n + H infinitely often, so liminf(p_{n+m} − p_n) ≪ k log k ≪ m³e^{4m}.
acceptance: Under Elliott–Halberstam the bound improves to O(m³e^{2m}) (Maynard, p. 385); that is not planned here.

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: A positive proportion of admissible m-tuples are prime (Maynard Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: For every m ≥ 1 there are r₀ and c > 0 such that every set A of r ≥ r₀ distinct nonnegative integers has at least c·C(r,m) subsets {h₁,…,h_m} ⊆ A for which infinitely many n make every n + hᵢ prime.
hypotheses: The source allows arbitrary integers. Translating A by a constant changes neither count, so natural numbers suffice.
proofSteps: With k = ⌈Cm²e^{4m}⌉ as in Theorem 1.1, every admissible k-set contains an m-subset with infinitely many prime translates.
Thin A: for each prime p ≤ k, delete the residue class mod p with the fewest elements. The remainder A₂ has s ≥ r∏_{p≤k}(1 − 1/p) elements, and every k-subset of it is admissible.

Double count: each of the C(s,k) k-subsets contains a good m-subset, and each m-subset lies in C(s−m,k−m) of them. So there are at least C(s,k)/C(s−m,k−m) ≫_m s^m ≫_m r^m good m-subsets, while C(r,m) ≤ r^m.
acceptance: This is a positive-proportion statement, not the prime m-tuples conjecture for any given tuple.

sources.match: The theorem and its deduction.

nodes.title: Logarithmic sieve dimension
nodes.statement: HasLogSieveDimension(P,g,κ,C) means: for every real z≥2, Σ_{p∈P, p prime, p≤z} g(p) log p ≤ κ log z+C. The sum is finite. P is a fixed set of naturals and g is a fixed real function; constants do not depend on z or on an application population.
hypotheses: The predicate records only the displayed inequality. Positivity of g, κ and C are separate theorem hypotheses; it does not assert a local density or any distribution estimate. In Chapter 11 g(p)=ω(p)/p.
proofSteps: Use the finite prime set obtained by filtering naturals up to floor z. Quantify the bound over every real z≥2, not merely a single cutoff.
acceptance: A finite set at a single cutoff does not supply constants uniform across a varying prime family.

sources.match: A quantified version of the source logarithmic condition; explicit C replaces its bounded additive term.

nodes.title: Euler-product sieve dimension
nodes.statement: HasProductSieveDimension(P,g,κ,K) means: for every real 2≤w≤z, ∏_{p∈P, p prime, w≤p<z}(1−g(p))⁻¹ ≤ K (log z/log w)^κ.
hypotheses: All endpoint choices are part of the definition: p=w is included and p=z is excluded. The predicate alone does not require g(p)<1; every sieve theorem requires 0≤g(p)<1 separately.
proofSteps: Take the finite product over primes below ceil z and filter by w≤p. Use real powers and the strictly positive logarithm of w.
acceptance: Do not infer this product-ratio condition from the logarithmic condition without controlling primes with g(p) near one.

nodes.title: Truncated remainder mass
nodes.statement: For an existing BoundingSieve s and real D, remainderMass(s,D)=Σ_{d|s.prodPrimes, d<D}|s.rem(d)|. Divisors are positive; the cutoff is strict.
hypotheses: D can be any real. The sum is zero if D≤1. If D>1 it includes d=1 and hence the mass-normalization error.
proofSteps: Filter the native positive divisor finset and sum absolute values of the existing remainder.

nodes.title: Level of distribution of a sieve family
nodes.statement: HasSieveLevel(F,θ) for a fixed family F:real→BoundingSieve means θ>0, X_F(x)≥0 for all x≥2, and: for every A>0 there exist B>0,C>0,x₀≥2 such that for all x≥x₀, remainderMass(F(x), x^θ/(log x)^B)≤ C X_F(x)/(log x)^A.
hypotheses: F and θ are fixed before A is chosen. B,C,x₀ may depend on F,θ,A, not on the varying x. This is a weighted sieve-family predicate, not Maynard’s π-centred prime-distribution predicate.
proofSteps: Write out the order of quantifiers. Retain the absolute divisor sum, its strict cutoff and its mass-normalization remainder.
acceptance: An arbitrary coefficient level, a pointwise error without summed uniformity, or a negative approximate mass is not this condition.

sources.match: A worker-specified quantitative family interface for the source’s distribution requirement; the logarithmic parametrization is explicit, not attributed as a definition in the source.

nodes.title: Coefficient error controlled by remainder mass
nodes.statement: If L≥0, |c(d)|≤L on the divisors of P and c(d)=0 on every divisor d≥D, then s.errSum(c)≤L remainderMass(s,D).
hypotheses: s is a BoundingSieve; D is real and the cutoff is strict. This promotes the remainderMass API item used by Brun’s estimate.
proofSteps: Split the finite divisor sum by d<D. The complementary coefficients vanish. Bound each remaining nonnegative term by L|R_d| and factor the constant out.
acceptance: D≤1 forces every contributing coefficient to vanish; L=0 gives zero error.

sources.match: Exact coefficient-sensitive native form, without a claim that truncation proves distribution.

nodes.title: Finite tilted density Euler product
nodes.statement: For any real a and BoundingSieve s, Σ_{d|P} ν(d)d^a = ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^a).
hypotheses: P=s.prodPrimes is nonzero squarefree; all powers have positive natural bases, including d=1.
proofSteps: Use the native squarefree-divisor/subset correspondence. Multiplicativity of ν and real powers on positive products identify each subset term. Expand the finite product by choosing either 1 or ν(p)p^a at each prime.
acceptance: P=1 gives 1=1 for every a; a=0 gives Σν(d)=∏(1+ν(p)).

sources.match: The squarefree weighted analogue of the Euler-product expansion, derived on the existing carrier.

nodes.title: Weighted Rankin cutoff bound
nodes.statement: For x>0 and σ≥0, Σ_{d|P, d≤x} dν(d) ≤ x^σ ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^(1−σ)).
hypotheses: s is a BoundingSieve. The inclusive cutoff is explicit; x<1 gives an empty sum.
proofSteps: For d≤x compare d^σ≤x^σ, multiply by ν(d)d^(1−σ), and sum. Extend the sum by nonnegative terms and apply the finite Euler-moment identity with exponent 1−σ.
acceptance: σ=0 remains valid; x=1 retains the d=1 contribution; do not include d=0.

sources.match: Explicit finite weighted Rankin inequality; no smooth-number carrier or asymptotic estimate is redefined.

nodes.title: Weighted Rankin remainder-tail bound
nodes.statement: For x>0 and a≥0, Σ_{d|P, x<d} ν(d) ≤ x^(−a) ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^a).
hypotheses: s is a BoundingSieve; the tail is strict.
proofSteps: On the tail use 1≤(d/x)^a, retain nonnegative ν(d), and extend to all divisors. Apply the Euler-moment identity.
acceptance: At x=P the tail is empty; x<1 includes d=1; a=0 gives the full density sum as an upper bound.

sources.match: A finite Rankin replacement for the integral tail route, with all parameters and endpoints explicit.

nodes.title: Tilted Euler-product estimate from logarithmic dimension
nodes.statement: Fix a set P and function g, with κ>0,C≥0, nonnegative g(p) for selected primes and HasLogSieveDimension(P,g,κ,C). There exist K>0,z₀≥exp(2) such that for every z≥z₀, ∏_{p∈P,p prime,p≤z}(1+g(p)p^(1/log z)) ≤ K(log z)^κ.
hypotheses: All data P,g,κ,C are fixed before K,z₀ are chosen. The constants are independent of z and of every application population.
proofSteps: Set A(t)=Σ_{p≤t,p∈P}g(p)log p. Apply the native Abel formula on [2,z] to 1/log t, isolating p=2, to obtain Σg(p)≤κ log log z+O_{κ,C}(1). Its derivative is −1/(t(log t)²), integrable on this domain.
For α=1/log z and 2≤p≤z, use exp(u)−1≤exp(1)u for 0≤u=α log p≤1. Thus Σg(p)(p^α−1)≤exp(1)(κ+C/log z), uniformly bounded.

Extend the finite summand by zero off the selected primes before using Real.prod_one_add_le_exp_sum, whose input is globally nonnegative. Exponentiate the two bounds and absorb only fixed constants in K.
acceptance: The lower endpoint is at least exp(2), so 0<1−1/log z<1 in the cutoff applications. No Mertens theorem is required when the logarithmic condition is given.

sources.match: Explicit proof route for the Euler product used in the weighted Rankin exercise; the proof is specified, not implemented.

nodes.title: Dimension-controlled weighted divisor count
nodes.statement: For fixed data of log-dimension-euler-bound, there exist K>0,z₀≥exp(2) such that for every z≥z₀, every x>0 and every BoundingSieve s whose prime factors are exactly the selected primes p≤z and whose ν(p)=g(p), Σ_{d|P_s,d≤x}dν(d) ≤ K x(log z)^κ exp(−log x/log z).
hypotheses: Constants are uniform in x and s; all density data and dimension constants are fixed. This implies the strict-cutoff version of source Lemma 11.7.
proofSteps: Apply weighted Rankin with σ=1−1/log z, then bound its finite Euler product by the preceding theorem. Rewrite x^σ as x exp(−log x/log z).
acceptance: The inclusive cutoff is a stronger conclusion than the source’s d<x; x<1 gives an empty divisor sum.

sources.match: Same weighted sum with ω(d)=dν(d); preserves every uniform parameter.

nodes.title: Dimension-controlled divisor-density tail
nodes.statement: For the same fixed data there exist K>0,z₀≥exp(2) such that for every z≥z₀,x>0 and matching sieve s, Σ_{d|P_s,x<d}ν(d) ≤ K(log z)^κ exp(−log x/log z).
hypotheses: For a fixed L>0 replace x by Lx and absorb the bounded factor L^(−1/log z) in K.
proofSteps: Use weighted Rankin with a=1/log z and the tilted Euler-product estimate. This avoids integration of a divisor-count bound and so removes the extra log z loss of the source integral argument.
acceptance: This is a worker-derived stronger finite-tail estimate, not a quotation of the source’s (log z)^(κ+1) bound. No infinite divisor tail is asserted.

sources.match: The same finite tail, bounded directly by Rankin instead of the stated integral route.

nodes.title: Eratosthenes estimate with a justified mass and divisor cutoff
nodes.statement: Let x>0,c,M≥0 and 0<σ<1. If 0≤X≤Mx, |R_d|≤c dν(d) for divisors d≤x, and A_d=0 for divisors d>x, then |S−X∏_{p|P}(1−ν(p))|≤(c+M)x^σ∏_{p|P}(1+ν(p)p^(1−σ)).
hypotheses: s is the native BoundingSieve; A_d is its weighted multSum. The mass bound and the divisor cutoff are assumptions to prove in an application, never consequences of the residue-label representation.
proofSteps: Split the native absolute Legendre remainder into d≤x and d>x. Bound the first piece by c times the weighted prefix. On the tail, A_d=0 gives |R_d|=Xν(d); apply weighted Rankin with a=1−σ and X≤Mx. Combine the common Euler product.
With σ=1−1/log z and the dimension estimate obtain O_{fixed data,c,M}(x(log z)^κ exp(−log x/log z)).
acceptance: This conditional statement does not claim the exact advertised Theorem 11.9 under its weaker printed hypotheses, nor does it fix the two-residue cutoff gap E7 in the Brun application.

sources.locator: §11.4, Theorem 11.9 and Exercise 11.6.3; proof of Theorem 11.11

nodes.title: Brun combinatorial coefficients
nodes.statement: For squarefree P, y>1, β>1 and parity ε∈{0,1}, put λ_ε(d)=μ(d) if d|P and the decreasing prime factors p₁>⋯>p_r of d satisfy p_m<(y/(p₁⋯p_m))^(1/β) for every 1≤m≤r with m≡ε mod 2; otherwise put λ_ε(d)=0. Put λ⁺=λ₁ and λ⁻=λ₀. The empty prime list makes λ⁺(1)=λ⁻(1)=1.
hypotheses: Only positive divisors contribute. Prefix p₁⋯p_m includes p_m. Both coefficient systems retain every admissible prefix, not just divisors whose whole number of prime factors has one parity.
proofSteps: Sort the native finite prime-factor set decreasingly. Test the specified one-based prefix constraints, then use the existing Möbius coefficient with its sign. Define zero outside the positive divisor finset.
acceptance: For P=6,y=100,β=2, both systems retain d=1,2,3,6 and agree with μ on those divisors. For P=6,y=4,β=2,z=4, λ⁺ retains only 1 whereas λ⁻ retains 1,2,3; the first-order lower sum is negative on the two-prime obstruction.

nodes.title: Brun pointwise divisor brackets
nodes.statement: For the Brun construction and every r|P, Σ_{d|r}λ⁻(d) ≤ 1_{r=1} ≤ Σ_{d|r}λ⁺(d). Hence Σ_{d|P}λ⁻(d)A_d≤S≤Σ_{d|P}λ⁺(d)A_d for nonnegative sample weights.

proofSteps: Use the decreasing-prime first-failure expansion of source Lemma 12.1 with the consistent strict prime cutoff and left-limit product at the last prime (E35), specialized to density one on the factors of r. Finite inclusion-exclusion leaves a sum of nonnegative first-failure contributions with the required parity sign. The combinatorial identity is polynomial and does not require the analytic strict-density hypothesis when specialized to one.
Apply the native-carrier weighted divisor interchange at each sample. Multiply both brackets by its nonnegative weight and sum.

nodes.title: Strict Brun coefficient support
nodes.statement: For squarefree P,y>1,β>1 and ε∈{0,1}, if every prime of P is <z≤y, then λ_ε(d)≠0 implies d<y.
hypotheses: The single-prime lower-coefficient exception is controlled by p<z≤y. The unit needs y>1.
proofSteps: For a nonempty decreasing list with last position of the required parity, its last prefix condition directly bounds the full product. Otherwise use the penultimate prefix condition and p_r<p_{r−1}≤p_{r−1}^β. Handle a one-prime lower list using the explicit prime cutoff; handle the empty list by y>1.

nodes.title: Dimension-controlled Brun main terms
nodes.statement: Let κ>0,K>1, β=9κ+1, u≥β,y>1,z=y^(1/u), all primes of P satisfy p<z, and g(p)=ν(p) on P and zero off P. Under HasProductSieveDimension(P,g,κ,K), with V=∏_{p|P}(1−ν(p)) and δ=exp(β−u)K^10, (1−δ)V ≤ mainSum(λ⁻) ≤ V ≤ mainSum(λ⁺) ≤ (1+δ)V.
hypotheses: P in the dimension predicate means the set of its prime factors. Strict prime-density bounds are supplied by BoundingSieve. The displayed non-strict inequalities include every degenerate empty-prime case.
proofSteps: Use the finite first-failure expansion with strict prime cutoffs and the last-prime left-limit product (E35): V⁺−V is the sum of odd-length failure masses, and V−V⁻ the sum of even-length failure masses. Each summand is nonnegative.

The prefix constraints give p_n≥z_n=z^(1−1/β)^n. Enlarge each summation domain; an ordered distinct-prime sum is at most the n-th power of the unrestricted prime sum divided by n!. The product-dimension bound controls V(z_n)/V(z); if z_n<2 use the identical empty-prime interval or the interval starting at 2.

Use the source’s b=9, a=exp(1+1/9)/9<exp(−1), its factorial bound n!≥exp(1)(n/exp(1))^n, and vanishing for n+β≤u. Sum the geometric tail to obtain δ. The lower main term has 1−δ, not the source display’s 1+δ (E33).
acceptance: δ may exceed one; then the lower bound can be negative and asserts no positive prime lower bound. Empty P gives V⁺=V⁻=V=1.

sources.match: Source estimate with the lower sign corrected from its first-failure proof.

nodes.title: Brun fundamental sieve estimate
nodes.statement: Under the Brun main-term hypotheses and X≥0, (1−δ)V X−remainderMass(s,y) ≤ S ≤ (1+δ)V X+remainderMass(s,y), where β=9κ+1,u≥β,z=y^(1/u), δ=exp(β−u)K^10.
hypotheses: This is the proved parameter range of this elementary combinatorial sieve. It is not a sharp beta-sieve theorem, a parity-breaking input or a Chen theorem.
proofSteps: Expand A_d=ν(d)X+R_d in both weighted brackets. The promoted modulus and support lemmas give |λ±|≤1 and support d<y. Apply the promoted remainder-mass error lemma, then multiply the main-term inequalities by nonnegative X.
acceptance: The range u≥9κ+1 and positivity of X are explicit. A positive sifted lower bound requires both δ<1 and a sufficiently small actual remainder mass.

sources.match: Exact weighted native-carrier form of the corrected combinatorial estimate.

nodes.title: From roughness to an almost-prime bound
nodes.statement: Let natural z≥2, n≠0 and k≥0. If every prime p dividing n satisfies z≤p and n<z^(k+1), then Nat.IsAtMostAlmostPrime(k,n).
hypotheses: Prime factors are counted with multiplicity. The upper bound is strict and the unit n=1 is allowed.
proofSteps: Every entry of the native prime factor list is at least z. Hence n, its product, is at least z raised to the list length Ω(n). If Ω(n)≥k+1, monotonicity of natural powers contradicts the strict upper bound. Use the existing at-most predicate, not the exact-k or distinct-factor predicate.
acceptance: n=8,z=2,k=2 violates the strict cutoff and has Ω=3 although it has only one distinct prime factor; n=1 gives Ω=0; n=0 is excluded.

sources.match: Exact endpoint-safe form of the source’s elementary prime-factor transfer. It supplies no sifted count or advanced-sieve analytic input.
